_note: Age in weeks. Each milestone has: id, age_weeks_start, age_weeks_end, title, body, urgency (normal|high|critical), playbook (feeding|sleep|potty-training|tantrum|screen-time), todos[]

milestones.title: Solid foods window is opening
milestones.body: Between 4–6 months most babies show readiness for first foods. Breast milk or formula is still 90% of nutrition — solids are practice. Start with single-ingredient purees: sweet potato, peas, butternut squash. One new food every 3–4 days so you can spot reactions.
todos: Try one single-ingredient puree this week
Introduce one new food every 3–4 days
Never start before 4 months or after 6 months

milestones.title: ⚠️ Peanut introduction window — closes at 11 months
milestones.body: The LEAP study (New England Journal of Medicine) found that introducing peanuts between 4–11 months reduces peanut allergy risk by up to 80%. This is one of the most impactful things you can do for your child's long-term health. The window closes at 11 months. Mix a small amount of smooth peanut butter into puree. Check with your pediatrician first if there's family history of allergies.
todos: Check with pediatrician if family allergy history exists
Mix 1/4 tsp smooth peanut butter into fruit or vegetable puree
Watch for 20 minutes after first introduction
Introduce 3x/week to maintain tolerance

milestones.title: Introduce the top allergens now
milestones.body: 6–9 months is the window to introduce the 9 major allergens: peanuts, tree nuts, eggs, milk, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, sesame. Introducing them early, while the immune system is still developing, significantly reduces lifetime allergy risk. One at a time, 3–4 days apart.
todos: Introduce eggs (well-cooked scrambled or puree)
Introduce tree nuts (almond/cashew butter thinned in puree)
Introduce fish (pureed salmon or cod)
Introduce wheat (well-cooked pasta or bread)
Keep a food diary — note any reactions

milestones.title: Switch to whole cow's milk at 12 months
milestones.body: At 12 months, your baby can transition from formula or breast milk to whole cow's milk. Whole milk (not skim or 2%) provides the fat needed for brain development through age 2. Target: 16–24 oz per day. Do not give cow's milk before 12 months — the kidneys can't handle the protein load.
todos: Begin mixing whole milk with formula (3/4 formula, 1/4 milk) for one week
Gradually shift ratio over 2 weeks
Cap at 24 oz/day — more displaces solid food
No honey until 12 months (botulism risk)

milestones.title: 4-month sleep regression — it's coming
milestones.body: Around 4 months, your baby's sleep architecture permanently changes to match adult sleep cycles. This causes more frequent night wakings. It's not a setback — it's brain development. It typically lasts 2–6 weeks. This is also a signal that sleep training is approaching.
todos: Expect more night wakings — this is normal and temporary
Avoid creating new sleep associations during this window (feeding to sleep, rocking)
Prioritize your own rest — sleep when baby sleeps if possible
Start thinking about sleep training approach (we'll send a full guide at 6 months)

milestones.title: ⚠️ Sleep training window is open
milestones.body: 6 months is when most pediatricians and sleep researchers greenlight sleep training. Before 6 months, babies genuinely need night feeds. After 6 months, most don't — but the habit is there. The window from 6–9 months is ideal: old enough to self-soothe, young enough that habits haven't fully calcified. Waiting makes it harder, not easier.
todos: Choose your method: Ferber, Fading, Chair, or Pick-Up-Put-Down (playbook covers all 4)
Pick a 2-week window with no travel or disruptions
Establish a consistent bedtime routine (bath, book, bed)
Target bedtime: 7–8pm for most babies this age
Brief your partner — consistency is everything

milestones.title: Watch for the 3-to-2 nap transition
milestones.body: Between 8–10 months, most babies are ready to drop from 3 naps to 2. Signs: third nap becomes a fight, bedtime gets harder, or the third nap is pushing bedtime past 8:30pm. Don't rush it — follow your baby's lead. The transition usually takes 2–4 weeks.
todos: Watch for short or refused third nap as the signal
Shift to 2 naps gradually — extend wake windows by 15 min/day
Protect morning nap (usually drops last)
Expect some overtiredness during the transition — it's temporary

milestones.title: The 2-to-1 nap transition is coming
milestones.body: Between 15–18 months, most toddlers transition from 2 naps to 1. This is one of the most disruptive sleep transitions. The one-nap day is longer (1.5–3 hours at midday). The transition often causes temporary overtiredness and earlier bedtimes.
todos: Sign: baby refuses or delays one of the two naps consistently for 2+ weeks
Shift nap to midday (11:30am–12pm start)
Move bedtime earlier during transition (6:30–7pm temporarily)
Give it 4–6 weeks to stabilize

milestones.title: Potty training readiness window is opening
milestones.body: The optimal window for potty training is 18–24 months. Starting in this window correlates with faster training (average 3–5 days using evidence-based methods), fewer accidents, and less regression. Starting too early (before 18 months) is usually ineffective. Starting too late (after 3 years) is harder because independent behaviors are more entrenched.
todos: Watch for readiness signs: staying dry 2+ hours, interest in toilet, hiding to poop
Introduce the potty as a concept (let them sit on it clothed first)
Read the Potty Training Playbook — it covers the 3-day method in detail
Clear your calendar for a 3-day training weekend

milestones.title: Tantrum peak is starting
milestones.body: 18 months to 3 years is peak tantrum territory. This isn't bad parenting — it's brain development. The prefrontal cortex (emotional regulation) is nowhere near developed. Your child genuinely cannot control these emotions yet. But how you respond now sets patterns that last for years.
todos: Learn the difference between a meltdown (overwhelmed) and a tantrum (testing limits) — responses differ
Practice the CALM method: Connect → Acknowledge → Limit → Move on
Remove the audience — tantrums escalate when they get a reaction
Never negotiate during a tantrum — wait for the storm to pass

milestones.title: Zero screens — the rule that matters most right now
milestones.body: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends no screen time before 18–24 months except video calls. This isn't about the content — it's about what screens displace. Every minute of screen time is a minute not spent in face-to-face interaction, which is irreplaceable for language and social development. Background TV counts.
todos: Video calls (FaceTime, Zoom) are the only screen exception
Background TV counts — turn it off when baby is in the room
Your screen time matters too — babies watch your face, not your phone

milestones.title: Approaching the screen time transition
milestones.body: At 18–24 months, the AAP allows limited high-quality screen time (1 hour/day max). But 'high quality' means: educational, co-viewed with a parent, and interactive. At this age, toddlers still can't transfer what they see on screen to real life without a parent bridging it. Watch with them. Talk about it.
todos: If introducing screens, start with co-viewing only (you watch together)
Choose programs with slow pacing and repetition (not fast cuts)
Avoid screens during meals and 1 hour before bed
Keep total screen time under 1 hour/day

milestones.title: Screen time habits form permanently now
milestones.body: Ages 2–4 are when screen time habits calcify. The patterns you establish now — what they watch, how long, when, and whether you're present — will be much harder to change at age 5, 6, or 7. This is the window to build healthy digital habits intentionally.
todos: Set a consistent daily limit and stick to it (1 hour max for under 5s)
Create screen-free zones: bedrooms, dinner table
Use screens as a planned activity, not a pacifier
Have a 'screen-off' routine — transition activity when time is up
